note: Seven adjudicated accidental variants: one capital accent, one comma, and the five words the hand missal sets in display capitals to mark the genuflection. Substantive text agrees across both witnesses with zero divergence — 189 tokens, letter for letter.

adjudicated.ruling: House rule (ORTHOGRAPHY.md): accents ARE printed on capitals. Óm-ni-a has three syllables and carries its accent; do omits accents on capitals throughout, and handmissal-eo attests the practice, as at ordinarium.confiteor-sacerdotis w038.

No comma before the relative, with handmissal-eo and with the corpus rulings at ordinarium.introibo w015 and ordinarium.quid-retribuam w005. Qui credunt in nómine ejus says which his are meant — it picks out those who believe, and cannot be lifted out of the sentence.

Ordinary capitalization, with do. Handmissal-eo sets the five words of the genuflection phrase in display capitals to catch the eye of a reader who must kneel at them; that is typography, not a reading, and ORTHOGRAPHY.md keeps display capitals out of running text. The same ruling governs w167, w168, w169 and w170.

Ordinary capitalization, as at w166, and the comma with do. The sentence does not end here: et habitávit in nobis continues it, and handmissal-eo leaves the phrase unpointed only because it breaks the line after it.
